```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(rqti)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Maxima exercises calculate question values and correct answers when an exercise
is instantiated. One exported item can therefore produce many random variants.
You can write the calculations in a `{maxima}` chunk, display their outputs with
`template_value()`, and bind a correct answer with
`gap_numeric(solution_variable = ...)` or `gap_text(solution_variable = ...)`.

This article describes the experimental `prototype/maxima-rmd` branch. Install
that version with R >= 4.1, then restart your RStudio R session:

```{r install}
remotes::install_github("shevandrin/rqti", ref = "prototype/maxima-rmd")
```

## Requirements

Install native Maxima separately and put its executable on PATH. In R,
`Sys.which("maxima")` should return a path. You can also set
`options(rqti.maxima = "/path/to/maxima")` to choose an executable explicitly.
No additional R interface package is required. Ordinary rqti exercises do not
require Maxima.

On Windows, choose the command-line launcher provided by your Maxima
installation. Its name and location depend on the installation; use a path
you have verified locally. Use forward slashes (or doubled backslashes in an
R string), without adding shell quotes around the path. Explicit file paths
are checked directly instead of being looked up with `Sys.which()`.

Set the option **before** starting the server: `start_server()`
passes that choice to RStudio's separate Knit session. Restart the server after
changing it. Running `options()` in the console alone does not set an option in
a separate R session.

The [Windows configuration problem reported in issue #257](https://github.com/shevandrin/rqti/issues/257#issuecomment-6360719800)
has not yet been reproduced on Windows. An explicit launcher path is a
configuration option; it is not a confirmed workaround for that report.

rqti runs Maxima locally when checking Rmd chunks and generating previews.
An exported exercise needs a delivery platform that supports the ONYX `MAXIMA`
custom operator, such as ONYX/OPAL. The XML retains the program; the sample values
from the authoring check are not fixed into the exported question.

## Write an Rmd exercise

Here is the complete addition example shipped with this branch:

```{r show-example, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
example_file <- system.file("extdata", "maxima-local-addition.Rmd", package = "rqti")
cat("````markdown\n", paste(readLines(example_file), collapse = "\n"), "\n````\n", sep = "")
```

The Maxima block returns a string containing a named association list:
`string(['a = a, 'b = b, 'answer = answer])`. rqti reads the output names and
types from one local execution, creates the template declarations, and keeps
the calculation in the QTI template. `template_value("a")` displays an output;
`gap_numeric(solution_variable = "answer")` uses the generated numeric answer.
`numericGap(solution_variable = ...)` provides the same binding in the S4 API.

## Preview in RStudio

Start the preview server in the RStudio console before clicking **Knit**. Copy
the installed example to a writable location first:

```{r preview}
library(rqti)
rqti::start_server()
example <- file.path(tempdir(), "maxima-addition.Rmd")
file.copy(
  system.file("extdata", "maxima-local-addition.Rmd", package = "rqti"),
  example,
  overwrite = TRUE
)
rstudioapi::navigateToFile(example)
```

Click **Knit**. The RStudio Viewer should show the addition exercise with
generated numbers. The preview also works in an external browser using the URL
printed by `start_server()` or `render_qtijs()`.

qti.js sends the template calculation to the local R server, which runs Maxima
and returns typed outputs. Submitting an answer preserves the current numbers;
reload the preview page to generate another variant. A failed preview shows the
diagnostic and a **Retry** button. To stop the server, use `rqti::stop_server()`.

The Knit button uses a separate R session. rqti passes both the server URL and
its renderer folder to that session, including when the console uses a
development checkout and Knit loads the installed package.

## Output types and authoring checks

Supported output types are `integer`, `float`, and `string`. Rational numbers
and real numeric constants can be used as floating-point outputs. Inference
observes one random variant; specify types when they may vary between variants:

For example, replace the addition chunk above with this explicitly typed chunk:

```{r show-explicit-types, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
cat(paste(c(
  "````markdown",
  "```{maxima addition, variables = c(a = \"integer\", b = \"integer\", answer = \"float\", label = \"string\")}",
  "block(",
  "    [a, b, answer, label],",
  "    a: random(100),",
  "    b: random(100),",
  "    answer: a + b,",
  "    label: \"Addition\",",
  "    string(['a = a, 'b = b, 'answer = answer, 'label = label])",
  ");",
  "```",
  "````"
), collapse = "\n"), "\n")
```

The named `variables` vector sets the QTI types for the returned outputs.
`answer = "float"` accepts both integer and floating-point results. The extra
text output can be displayed with `template_value("label")`. Explicit types do
not bypass the local execution check.

Lists and other structured values need an explicit `string` declaration when
used for display. This does not create a generated image.

### Text answers

Use `gap_text(solution_variable = "answer")` when the Maxima output is a
`string`. The output supplies one correct text answer for each attempt;
submitting an answer preserves the generated word. Matching ignores case by
default; set `case_sensitive = TRUE` to require matching capitalization.
The entire string must match, including spaces and punctuation. Dynamic text
answers do not support spelling tolerance or a list of alternative answers.
`textGap(solution_variable = "answer")` provides the same binding in the S4 API.

This example can be previewed in qti.js and exported for ONYX/OPAL:

```{r show-text-example, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
text_file <- system.file("extdata", "maxima-text-answer.Rmd", package = "rqti")
cat("````markdown\n", paste(readLines(text_file), collapse = "\n"), "\n````\n", sep = "")
```

To try it, copy the installed example to a writable location, start the preview
server, and open the copy in RStudio:

```{r preview-text}
example <- file.path(tempdir(), "maxima-text-answer.Rmd")
file.copy(
  system.file("extdata", "maxima-text-answer.Rmd", package = "rqti"),
  example,
  overwrite = TRUE
)
rqti::start_server()
rstudioapi::navigateToFile(example)
```

Click **Knit**. Copying the word in lowercase earns one point; copying its
capitalization exactly into both gaps earns two. Wrong or empty answers earn
zero. Submitting preserves the word; reloading generates another variant.
These cases have been tested with native Maxima in qti.js, including Unicode,
punctuation, and numeric-looking strings such as `"0"` and `"01"`.
The ONYX/OPAL export validates against the extended schema; live OPAL scoring
for generated text answers still needs verification.

### Display LaTeX strings

Return LaTeX as a Maxima string. The following forms have been checked in a
fresh ONYX/OPAL attempt and after answer submission:

* Inline math: put `\\(` and `\\)` around the inline `template_value()` reference
  in Markdown (try 5 in the original example).
* Display math: put `$$` around the reference (try 6).
* Self-contained inline math: return a string including `\\(` and `\\)` in
  Maxima, then insert the reference directly (`tex_embedded`).

The [OPAL LaTeX test](https://bildungsportal.sachsen.de/opal/auth/RepositoryEntry/56806965249)
contains the original tries. Tries 5, 6, and `tex_embedded` render correctly;
the local qti.js preview supports these forms too.

Backslashes in a literal **Maxima string** must be doubled: `"\\mathbb{R}"`
produces `\mathbb{R}`. The doubled backslashes in Markdown's `\\(...\\)`
likewise preserve the math delimiters; a single `\(` in Markdown loses its
backslash during conversion.

The local preview typesets the completed Maxima output and preserves it when
answers are submitted. The exported XML keeps live `printedVariable`
references, including those inside math, rather than the sample values from
the local check. Rmd references are inserted without an extra HTML span, so
ONYX can substitute the values without interrupting the surrounding formula.
To put the delimiters inside the generated value itself instead, use the
`embedded` output below.

The complete example shows all three forms:

```{r show-latex-example, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
latex_file <- system.file("extdata", "maxima-latex.Rmd", package = "rqti")
cat("````markdown\n", paste(readLines(latex_file), collapse = "\n"), "\n````\n", sep = "")
```

rqti executes each Rmd Maxima chunk before export, including chunks with explicit
types. Syntax/runtime errors, missing outputs, incompatible declared types, or
missing template references stop export. Diagnostics identify the source file,
chunk label, and numbered code. Template chunks must be evaluated and uncached.
Only one Maxima chunk is allowed per Rmd exercise. Return all the values
needed by the question and its answer from that chunk's `string([...])` list.
This follows the all-in-one approach in
[issue #257](https://github.com/shevandrin/rqti/issues/257): independent ONYX
calculations may run in parallel and give separate random calculations the same
seed. A single block keeps related calculations together. Displayed references
are supported in the question body.

### Check Maxima code directly

`maxima_check()` takes one R character string containing Maxima code, including
its terminating semicolons or dollar signs. It runs that code in a fresh local
Maxima process and returns `TRUE` invisibly on success:

```{r check-program}
rqti::maxima_check("1 + 2;")
```

For a program returning the same `string([...])` associations used in an Rmd
chunk, set `outputs = TRUE` to obtain a named vector of inferred types:

```{r check-outputs}
code <- "string(['a = 3, 'answer = 1/2, 'label = \"Addition\"]);"
types <- rqti::maxima_check(code, outputs = TRUE)
types
# c(a = "integer", answer = "float", label = "string")
```

A syntax or runtime failure raises an R error containing the Maxima diagnostic
and numbered source code. Rmd conversion calls this function automatically;
you do not need to call it separately before knitting. Execution is bounded by
`options(rqti.maxima_timeout = 120)` in seconds, including library startup.
The statistics libraries `distrib`, `descriptive`, and `stats` load by default.

## Export and validate

```{r export}
xml <- rqti::rmd2xml(example, path = tempdir())
result <- rqti::verify_qti(xml, schema = "extended", ignore_import = FALSE)
stopifnot(result$valid)
rqti::rmd2zip(example, path = tempdir())
```

**Choose `schema = "extended"` for ONYX Maxima items.** The standard QTI 2.1
schema rejects ONYX's `customOperator/@value` attribute and the
`setCorrectResponse` rule in response processing. The default `verify_qti(xml)`
therefore reports these items as invalid. rqti's extended schema accepts those
extensions while still checking the XML structure.

Schema validation does not execute the Maxima program or prove that every
random variant works. Rmd authoring checks run one variant locally; preview
scoring and an import into the target ONYX installation provide further checks.

## Compiled library cache

The first calculation can take longer while Maxima compiles its libraries.
Authoring checks and previews share compiled libraries in rqti's managed user
cache across R sessions. Each calculation still starts a fresh Maxima process;
programs, variables, and answers remain independent and temporary.

Build changes invalidate the cache. Old builds, caches unused for 30 days,
incomplete library loads, and caches exceeding 64 MiB are removed automatically.
Concurrent sessions coordinate through a lock. You can choose another cache
directory or keep the cache within the current R session:

```{r cache}
options(rqti.maxima_cache_dir = "/path/to/cache")
options(rqti.maxima_cache_dir = FALSE)
```
